paragraphs: The verse “Hashem Melech” (Hashem reigns), etc., must be doubled, in the manner that Israel doubled it when they said, “Hashem, He is God; Hashem, He is God” (I Kings 18:39). The reason is to proclaim His kingship over both bodies and souls, and this is also explained in the Tikkunim regarding the secret of this verse, which states that for this reason they doubled it twice. It must be said standing, together with the verse “Vehayah Hashem LeMelech,” etc. And even if an individual is not praying with the congregation, but is reciting the Shema and its blessings, when the congregation says “Hashem Melech,” etc., he must stand, though he need not stop to answer with them — even if he is standing within the Korbanot section, where interruption is permitted, as explained in the words of our teacher [the Ari], of blessed memory, in Sha’ar HaKavanot. However, if he is not engaged with the Kavanot of the prayers, but is silent, or is engaged in Torah study, it is proper that he too join the congregation and answer with them. The verse “Hashem Melech” that occurs within the verses of “Yehi Chevod” does not need to be said standing, and does not need to be doubled.

clarification.explanation: The verse “Hashem Melech” (recited at the beginning of the prayers, before Baruch She’amar) should be said twice in succession, similar to the way Israel doubled it and said “Hashem, He is God; Hashem, He is God” at Mount Carmel. The reason is to proclaim Hashem’s kingship over both the body and the soul, as is also explained in the Book of Tikkunim. It should be said standing, together with the verse “Vehayah Hashem LeMelech,” etc. Even an individual who is not praying with the congregation but is reciting the Shema and its blessings must stand when the congregation says “Hashem Melech,” though he is not obligated to stop and answer with them — even if he is in the “Korbanot” section, where pausing is permitted. However, one who is not engaged with the intentions of the prayer but is silent or studying Torah should join the congregation and answer with them. The verse “Hashem Melech” that appears within the verses of “Yehi Chevod” does not require standing or doubling.
takeaways: ‘Hashem Melech,’ recited before Baruch She’amar, should be said twice while standing, to proclaim Hashem’s kingship over both body and soul.
One who is in the midst of the Shema and its blessings must stand when hearing this from the congregation, but is not obligated to stop and answer.
The verse ‘Hashem Melech’ within ‘Yehi Chevod’ does not require standing or doubling.

paragraphs: The verses of “Hashem Melech,” etc., said in Selichot — I have derived, with the help of Heaven, in my holy work Makabtziel, that they must be said standing, and the listener too must stand, following the law stated above regarding the verse “Hashem Melech” said before Baruch She’amar. This is because the Arizal, of blessed memory, in Sha’ar HaKavanot, gave a reason for standing at this verse: it is the secret of the ten sefirot of the World of Asiyah, which include Arich Anpin, Abba and Imma, and Zachar and Nekevah — see there. And in the siddur of the Rashash, of blessed memory, for Selichot, these kavanot were arranged for this verse in Selichot as well, so they correspond in their placement. However, I raised a doubt there regarding the verse “Hashem Melech,” etc., said during the Hakafot of Hoshana Rabbah and Simchat Torah, whether one must stand — since the congregation is standing anyway [while circling] — but the doubt concerns a person sitting in the synagogue who is not circling with the congregation, whether he must stand when “Hashem Melech” is said. My opinion inclines that he is not obligated to stand, because in the Hakafot this is said merely as a custom, and the kavanot relevant to the verse are not present there; and since this kavanah is absent, another person sitting in the synagogue likewise need not stand.

clarification.explanation: The verses of “Hashem Melech” recited during Selichot must also be said standing, and the listener must stand as well — like the law regarding the verse said before Baruch She’amar — because the Arizal gave a reason for standing at this verse: it secretly expresses the ten sefirot of the World of Asiyah, including the aspects of Arich Anpin, Abba and Imma, and Zachar and Nekevah. In the Rashash’s siddur, special kavanot were likewise set for this verse in Selichot, so they correspond in their placement. Regarding the verse “Hashem Melech” said during the Hakafot of Hoshana Rabbah and Simchat Torah, the Ben Ish Chai leaves it in doubt whether one must stand, because during the Hakafot the congregation is already standing and circling in any case — but a person sitting in the synagogue who is not circling with the congregation, in his view, is not obligated to stand, because there the secret kavanot attached to the verse are absent, and it is merely an ordinary custom.
takeaways: The verses of ‘Hashem Melech’ in Selichot likewise require standing, based on the kabbalistic intention they carry — the secret of the ten sefirot of the World of Asiyah (Arich Anpin, Abba and Imma, Zachar and Nekevah) — the same law as before Baruch She’amar.
During the Hakafot of Hoshana Rabbah and Simchat Torah, one who is not circling with the congregation is not obligated to stand, since those kavanot are not present there.

paragraphs: On Shabbat and Yom Tov, the custom in several places is for children to stand at the reader’s platform (teivah) and recite the zemirot aloud, from the beginning of “Hodu” until the end of the Song [at the Sea]. Nevertheless, one must be careful that the recitation of “Hashem Melech,” etc., be said by the prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) aloud, just as with Baruch She’amar, with the congregation answering after him — and such is the custom in our city of Baghdad. See Minchat Aharon, page 16, column b. Therefore, in places where it was customary for children to say it, the custom should be changed so that the prayer leader says it; and if the prayer leader has not yet arrived, another distinguished adult should say it.

clarification.explanation: On Shabbat and Yom Tov there are places where children stand near the platform and recite the zemirot aloud, from the beginning of “Hodu” until the end of the Song at the Sea. However, one must be careful: the verse “Hashem Melech” (before Baruch She’amar) must specifically be said by the prayer leader aloud, just like Baruch She’amar itself, with the congregation answering after him — and this is the custom in Baghdad. Therefore, in places where it was the custom for children to say it, the custom should be changed so that the prayer leader says it; and if the prayer leader has not yet arrived, another distinguished adult should say it instead.
takeaways: The verse ‘Hashem Melech’ before Baruch She’amar must specifically be said by the prayer leader aloud (not by children), with the congregation answering after him.

paragraphs: It is good to recite the psalm “Elohim Yechonenu Vivarecheinu” (Psalm 67) in the shape of the Menorah; mental visualization alone suffices if one does not have a diagram before him. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, the psalm “Hashamayim Mesaprim” is recited, and there is a secret in this matter. The pious ones in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt speedily, of the Midrash Beit El yeshivah, are accustomed to recite the psalm “Hashamayim” also on Chol HaMoed, as mentioned at the beginning of the book Divrei Shalom, in their [list of] customs. Here in our city of Baghdad, the custom on Chol HaMoed is to say “Yechonenu” and not to say “Hashamayim.” I, the servant [of Hashem], did not find it necessary to require them to change their custom in this regard, because I did not find this matter explicitly stated in the words of our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory, regarding Chol HaMoed — only regarding Shabbat and Yom Tov. And although the matter would seem reasonable according to the custom of the pious ones mentioned, nevertheless I left them with their custom. But I myself say “Yechonenu” together with them, and I also say “Hashamayim,” following the custom of the pious ones mentioned, and so it is fitting for every wise person to do.

clarification.explanation: It is good to recite the psalm “Elohim Yechonenu Vivarecheinu” (Psalm 67) while visualizing the shape of the Menorah in one’s mind (even without an actual diagram before him). On Shabbat and Yom Tov the psalm “Hashamayim Mesaprim” is also recited, and there is a secret reason for this. The pious ones of Jerusalem (Midrash Beit El) are accustomed to recite “Hashamayim Mesaprim” also on Chol HaMoed, as recorded in their customs. In Baghdad, the custom on Chol HaMoed is to say only “Yechonenu” without “Hashamayim Mesaprim,” and the Ben Ish Chai saw no need to change this custom, since he found no explicit source in the words of the Arizal regarding Chol HaMoed (only regarding Shabbat and Yom Tov). Nevertheless, he himself was accustomed to say both psalms even on Chol HaMoed — “Yechonenu” (following the local custom) and “Hashamayim Mesaprim” (following the custom of the pious ones) — and he recommends that every wise person do the same.
takeaways: The psalm ‘Elohim Yechonenu’ is recited while visualizing the shape of the Menorah in the mind; the psalm ‘Hashamayim Mesaprim’ is recited on Shabbat and Yom Tov for a secret reason.
Customs differ between Baghdad and Jerusalem regarding Chol HaMoed; the Ben Ish Chai recommends reciting both psalms together even on Chol HaMoed.

paragraphs: These psalms of “Rannu,” which are added on Shabbat and Yom Tov, contain great secrets, and one must be careful in their recitation, for their level is exceedingly exalted. The first two psalms, “Rannu” and “Beshanoto” [i.e., “LeDavid Beshanoto”], each contain twenty-two verses, corresponding to the twenty-two letters of the Torah, and 161 words, corresponding to the numerical value of the Name ‘Ehyeh’ spelled out with the letter yud. Also, in “Rannu” there are thirteen occurrences of the Name Havayah, corresponding to the Thirteen Attributes [of Mercy], as mentioned in the siddur of the Rashash, of blessed memory. If so, open your eyes and see — take great care in their recitation, for if a single word is missing, one loses much good, Heaven forbid. And regarding the fact that the letter vav is missing from “LeDavid Beshanoto” [compared to the parallel text in Samuel], King David himself later completed it in the verse “Podeh Hashem” (Psalm 34:23), because vav, by the Atbash cipher, is interchangeable with peh. In my responsum in my holy work Rav Pe’alim, I explained the reasons for this based on the holy Zohar, Terumah, page 137, and the words of our teacher [the Arizal], of blessed memory, in Sefer Peri Etz Chaim.

clarification.explanation: The additional psalms recited on Shabbat and Yom Tov (beginning with “Rannu”) contain great secrets, and one must take great care in reciting them precisely because of their exalted level. The first two psalms — “Rannu” and “LeDavid Beshanoto” — each contain twenty-two verses, corresponding to the twenty-two letters of the Torah, and each contains 161 words, corresponding to the numerical value of the holy Name ‘Ehyeh’ spelled out with the letter yud. In the psalm “Rannu” there are also thirteen occurrences of the Name Havayah, corresponding to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. Therefore one must be very careful to recite them precisely — if a single word is missing, one forfeits much goodness, Heaven forbid. The Ben Ish Chai notes that in the psalm “LeDavid Beshanoto” the letter vav is missing (compared to the parallel verse in the Book of Samuel), and King David himself completed this in another verse (“Podeh Hashem”), because according to a certain cipher (Atbash) the letter vav is interchangeable with peh — and he explains this in greater depth in his work Rav Pe’alim, based on the holy Zohar.
takeaways: One must be careful to recite the psalms ‘Rannu’ and ‘LeDavid Beshanoto’ precisely, word for word, because of the numerical secrets contained in them.
These psalms are numerically connected to the holy Name ‘Ehyeh’ and to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy.

paragraphs: The verse “Vayehi Noam” contains deep and exalted intentions, and one must at least intend its plain meaning, for its intention according to the Zohar is: even though we do not know how to intend the secret meanings of the mitzvot and prayers, Hashem, may He be blessed, will complete our intention and credit us as though we had intended all the proper intentions; and through this, our actions in performing mitzvot and the movement of our lips in prayer will be able to ascend on high and accomplish their effect. And in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, it is explained that one must intend in this verse: that if we have sinned and thereby caused the light of holiness that was drawn upon us through good deeds to be removed, then You, God, in Your mercy, will rectify and restore those good deeds, and You will again draw upon us the light of that holiness. These two simple intentions a person should intend each time he recites this verse, before every mitzvah and engagement in Torah study. Some are meticulous to repeat this verse each time, so as to intend one intention on the first recitation and the second intention on the second recitation, and this is a fine custom, since in any case there is a reason for saying it twice. In all the communities of Israel it is customary to add on Yom Tov the psalm of that particular festival, but the pious ones of Beit El did not follow this custom.

clarification.explanation: The verse “Vayehi Noam” contains deep and exalted intentions, and at the very least one should intend its plain meaning. According to the Zohar, the simple intention is: even if we do not know how to intend all the secrets of the mitzvot and prayers, the Holy One, blessed be He, will complete our intention and credit it to us as though we had intended properly, so that our deeds and our prayers will ascend on high and accomplish their effect. According to the Rashash’s siddur, the second intention is: if we have sinned and thereby caused the removal of the light of holiness that used to be drawn upon us through good deeds, may Hashem in His mercy repair this and restore the flow of that light. These two simple intentions should be intended each time this verse is recited, before every mitzvah and Torah study. Some are accustomed to repeat the verse — one intention the first time and the second intention the second time — and this is a fine custom. In all the communities of Israel it is customary to add on Yom Tov the psalm specific to that festival, but the pious ones of Beit El did not follow this custom.
takeaways: In the verse ‘Vayehi Noam’ one should intend two main intentions: that Hashem complete what we lack in intention, and that He repair what we have damaged and again draw upon us the light of holiness.
Some are accustomed to repeat the recitation of the verse, one intention each time — a fine custom.

paragraphs: One should recite Baruch She’amar, whose text consists of 87 words, while standing; it is an exalted and lofty praise, instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly, based on a note that fell from heaven. As soon as one begins to say Baruch She’amar, he should hold the tzitzit of the two front corners [of his tallit] facing him, and they should remain in his hand until the end of Baruch She’amar, at which point he should kiss them and set them down. And one must say ‘al ha-beriyot,’ [with careful pronunciation:] the bet with a shva, the reish with a chirik, and the yud with a cholam. He should also say ‘bafeh imo’ [with the mouth, with him] and not ‘befi’ [with my mouth], as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: One should recite ‘Baruch She’amar,’ whose text contains 87 words, standing — an exalted and lofty praise instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly based on a note that fell from heaven. When beginning to say ‘Baruch She’amar,’ one should hold the tzitzit of the two front corners and keep them in hand until the end of the blessing, then kiss them and set them down. One must be precise in pronouncing the word ‘habriyot’ (the bet with a shva, the reish with a chirik, the yud with a cholam), and one should say ‘hamehulal befeh amo’ and not ‘befi amo.’
takeaways: Baruch She’amar is recited standing while holding the tzitzit of the two front corners until its end, at which point they are kissed.
One must be precise in pronouncing the word ‘habriyot’ (ha-B’RI-yot), and say ‘hamehulal befeh amo,’ not ‘befi.’

paragraphs: If a person finished Baruch She’amar before the cantor finished, he should hasten to say Mizmor LeTodah immediately, and answer Amen to the cantor’s blessing. But if he finished together with the cantor himself, he should not answer Amen, since that would be regarded as answering Amen to his own blessing, as mentioned by the Acharonim, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One who finishes reciting ‘Baruch She’amar’ before the cantor finishes should continue immediately to the psalm ‘LeTodah,’ and answer ‘Amen’ to the cantor’s blessing when he finishes. But one who finishes exactly together with the cantor should not answer ‘Amen,’ since this would be regarded as answering Amen to his own blessing (rather than someone else’s blessing).
takeaways: One who finishes Baruch She’amar before the cantor continues on and answers Amen to his blessing; one who finishes together with him does not answer Amen.

paragraphs: If one is saying Baruch She’amar, and has already begun to say the blessing [itself], ‘Baruch Atah Hashem Eloheinu Melech HaOlam,’ and hears Kaddish, Kedushah, or Barechu, he should pause to answer the entire Kaddish, from ‘Amen Yehei Shemei Rabba’ until ‘Be’alma.’ And although Maran, of blessed memory, ruled that one answers until ‘Yitbarach,’ I have proven in my holy work Makabtziel, from the words of our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory, in Sha’ar HaKavanot, that one should answer the whole of it, until ‘Be’alma,’ and this is the main [ruling]. He should likewise answer the first five ‘amens’ of the Kaddish, but the ‘amens’ of ‘Al Yisrael’ and ‘Yehei Shelama,’ and the ‘amens’ of blessings, he should not interrupt to answer aloud, but should only think them in his heart. Likewise he should answer only the two verses of Kedushah, ‘Kadosh’ and ‘Baruch,’ but the verse ‘Yimloch’ he should not answer, but should only think it in his heart. He should likewise answer ‘Baruch Hashem,’ etc., in the Kaddish of Barechu. And in Modim he should bow and answer only the three words ‘Modim Anachnu Lach,’ though some say [only] the word ‘Modim’ alone; and I, the servant [of Hashem], have determined in my holy works to answer these three words, ‘Modim Anachnu Lach’ — see further, Parashat Shemot, letter vav. All this applies if he has begun the blessing that is in the middle of Baruch She’amar, as explicitly written in Kaf HaChaim, siman 8, letter heh. But if he has not yet begun the blessing, and is still among the twelve [expressions of] ‘Baruch’ at the beginning — even though he has already begun them — he stops to answer everything that requires a response of sanctity, but then returns and says Baruch She’amar from its beginning to its end, so that he says these 87 words without adding any other word among them, because there is a secret in this number. The same law applies if, on Shabbat or Yom Tov, he mistakenly began Baruch She’amar before Rannu: if he has not yet said the blessings in the middle, he should say Rannu, and then say Baruch She’amar after it, in the proper order.

clarification.explanation: If a person has already begun the blessing itself within Baruch She’amar (‘Baruch Atah Hashem...’) and hears Kaddish, Kedushah, or Barechu, he should answer the entire Kaddish up to ‘Be’alma’ (rather than only until ‘Yitbarach,’ as Maran ruled), as the Ben Ish Chai demonstrated in his work Makabtziel from the words of the Arizal. He also answers the first five amens of the Kaddish, but the amens of ‘Al Yisrael’ and ‘Yehei Shelama,’ as well as the amens of blessings, he does not answer aloud but only thinks in his heart. In Kedushah he answers only the two verses ‘Kadosh’ and ‘Baruch,’ but not ‘Yimloch’ — that he only thinks in his heart. In the Kaddish following Barechu he answers ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach,’ and in Modim he bows and answers aloud only the three words ‘Modim Anachnu Lach’ (not the entire Modim d’Rabbanan text). All this applies when he has already begun the blessing itself in the middle of Baruch She’amar; but if he is still within the first twelve expressions of ‘Baruch’ (before the blessing itself), he should stop and answer everything requiring sanctification as usual, but then he must go back and recite all of Baruch She’amar from beginning to end, in order to say these exact 87 words without addition, because there is a secret in this precise count. The same law applies if, on Shabbat or Yom Tov, he mistakenly began Baruch She’amar before Rannu.
takeaways: Within the blessing of Baruch She’amar itself, one answers Kaddish up to ‘Be’alma’ and Kedushah only ‘Kadosh’ and ‘Baruch,’ and in Modim only ‘Modim Anachnu Lach’ — everything else only in silent thought.

If one is still within the first twelve expressions of ‘Baruch’ (before the blessing itself), he should stop and answer as usual, but then must go back and recite the whole of Baruch She’amar from the beginning, to preserve the exact word count.

paragraphs: Within Pesukei DeZimra, one should answer even the amens of [ordinary] blessings, for so testified our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, concerning our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory: that he would answer Amen to blessings even in the midst of the zemirot. But he did not explain to us regarding the amens of ‘Titkabel’ and ‘Al Yisrael veYehei Shelama.’ In my holy work Makabtziel I raised this as a doubt, and from the words of Rav Shalmei Tzibbur, page 85, column a, it appears that these amens are of a lesser status than the amens of blessings, though he did not explain this matter there explicitly. And from the words of Sefer HaKavanot, it may be inferred somewhat that it speaks specifically of amens of blessings. In the end, out of doubt, I concluded that refraining is preferable [sheiv ve’al ta’aseh adif]: these amens should be thought in the heart, and all the more so regarding ‘Baruch Hu U’Varuch Shemo,’ which should be thought and not answered aloud.

clarification.explanation: Within Pesukei DeZimra itself (between Baruch She’amar and Yishtabach), one should answer even amens of ordinary blessings aloud, as Rabbi Chaim Vital testified that he saw the Arizal answering Amen to blessings even in the middle of the zemirot. Regarding the amens of ‘Titkabel,’ ‘Al Yisrael,’ and ‘Yehei Shelama,’ no explicit explanation was given, and the Ben Ish Chai remained in doubt. Out of this doubt he rules stringently (‘refraining is preferable’): these amens should only be thought in the heart and not answered aloud, and all the more so ‘Baruch Hu U’Varuch Shemo.’
takeaways: Within Pesukei DeZimra one answers Amen aloud to ordinary blessings, but for the amens of ‘Titkabel,’ ‘Al Yisrael,’ and ‘Yehei Shelama’ — only silent thought, out of doubt.

paragraphs: The eighteen verses of ‘Yehi Chevod’ correspond to the eighteen letters of the six combinations of the Name Shaddai, and within these verses there are eighteen mentions [of the divine Name], alluding to the eighteen (Chai) worlds. After saying these eighteen verses, one should immediately say the two verses ‘Ashrei Yoshvei’ and ‘Ashrei Ha’am,’ and immediately after them, without delay, ‘Tehillah LeDavid Aromimcha,’ etc. One must be very careful not to interrupt between these verses and ‘Tehillah LeDavid Aromimcha’ with any other verse whatsoever, for this damages the crown formed by them for the attribute of Malchut. Therefore, if one sees that [the congregation] is about to begin Kaddish or Kedushah or the like, he should pause before completing the eighteen verses, in order to answer. And if he happens to be called upon suddenly to answer something requiring sanctification, so that he is forced to interrupt, I have written in my holy work Makabtziel that he should answer the Kaddish, Kedushah, and the like, even between ‘Ashrei’ and ‘Tehillah LeDavid’ — except that he must be careful, after answering, to go back and say the last three verses of ‘Yehi Chevod,’ and then continue with all the verses after them without interruption.

clarification.explanation: The eighteen verses of ‘Yehi Chevod’ are aligned with the eighteen letters of the six combinations of the holy Name Shaddai, and within these verses there are eighteen mentions of the divine Name (azkarot), alluding to the eighteen (Chai) worlds. After these eighteen verses one should immediately say the two verses ‘Ashrei Yoshvei’ and ‘Ashrei Ha’am,’ and immediately after them, without delay, ‘Tehillah LeDavid Aromimcha.’ One must be very careful not to interrupt anywhere in this sequence with any other verse, because interruption damages the spiritual ‘crown’ formed by them for the sefirah of Malchut. Therefore, if one sees that the congregation is about to begin Kaddish or Kedushah, it is better to pause before finishing the eighteen verses and answer there. If, nevertheless, one is forced to interrupt suddenly to answer something requiring sanctification in the middle (even between ‘Ashrei’ and ‘Tehillah LeDavid’), one should answer, but afterward must go back and repeat the last three verses of ‘Yehi Chevod’ before continuing on without interruption.
takeaways: One must not interrupt at all between the eighteen verses of ‘Yehi Chevod,’ ‘Ashrei Yoshvei,’ ‘Ashrei Ha’am,’ and ‘Tehillah LeDavid’ — this is one sequence that must not be marred.
If one is forced to interrupt to answer something requiring sanctification, one should answer and then go back and repeat the last three verses of ‘Yehi Chevod’ before continuing.

paragraphs: The verse ‘Poteach et Yadecha’ [Who opens Your hand] — one should intend, according to its plain meaning, that He, may He be blessed, is the One who watches over, feeds, and sustains all. One should also intend the holy Names alluded to within it, as recorded in the siddurim. And if one did not intend this verse even according to its plain meaning, he has not fulfilled his obligation, and must go back and say it again at the place where it is mentioned within Pesukei DeZimra, before the blessing of Yishtabach. And if he does not remember until after he has said the blessing of Yishtabach, he should say it after the conclusion of the Amidah, beginning from the verse ‘Somech Hashem,’ etc.; in this way he can rectify what was distorted, as mentioned in Chesed LeAlafim — see there. The custom here in our city, may it be protected, when saying the aforementioned verse ‘Poteach,’ is to spread the palms of the hands toward heaven, and this is a fine custom, performing a symbolic act to receive the flow [of sustenance] from above for their fortune. Similarly, in Chomat Anach, in [the commentary on] Divrei HaYamim, on the verse ‘and spread his hands toward heaven’ (II Chronicles 6:13), regarding King Solomon, peace be upon him — see there. And regarding what Rabbi Yehuda Tzarfati, of blessed memory, wrote in Yad Yosef, page 15, in the name of the Kabbalists, that when saying the verse ‘Poteach,’ etc., one must raise his hands upward, etc. — I cast doubt on this in my holy work Makabtziel, based on the holy Zohar, that one should not raise his hands except for washing the hands and for the Priestly Blessing, and where it is said [to raise hands], it is said [only there]; rather, spreading the palms without raising is correct. And in the manuscript Keter Malchut it is written that one should be very careful with the two psalms ‘Halelu et Hashem Min HaShamayim’ and ‘Halleluyah Halelu Kel BeKodsho,’ to say them slowly and with intention, for concerning them our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the Gemara: ‘May my portion be among those who complete the Hallel every day’ — see Rashi, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: In the verse ‘Poteach et Yadecha’ (within Ashrei), one should intend according to its plain meaning that Hashem is the One who watches over, feeds, and sustains all, and should also intend the holy Names alluded to within it as noted in the siddurim. One who did not intend this verse, even in its plain sense, has not fulfilled his obligation, and must return and say it again at the point where it is mentioned within Pesukei DeZimra, provided this is before the blessing of Yishtabach. If its time has already passed and he has said Yishtabach, he should say it after completing the Amidah, beginning from the verse ‘Somech Hashem.’ The local custom is to spread the palms upward when reciting the verse ‘Poteach,’ as a symbolic act of receiving the divine flow from above — as is mentioned regarding King Solomon, who spread his hands toward heaven. Some disagree with the suggestion to raise the hands upward for this verse, holding that raising the hands applies only to washing the hands and to the Priestly Blessing, while here spreading the palms without raising suffices. One should also be careful to recite the two psalms ‘Halelu et Hashem Min HaShamayim’ and ‘Halleluyah Halelu Kel BeKodsho’ slowly and with intention, since concerning their recitation it is stated in the Gemara: ‘May my portion be among those who complete the Hallel every day.’
takeaways: In the verse ‘Poteach et Yadecha’ one should intend the plain meaning (Hashem’s providence) and the holy Names; without this, one must repeat it where it is mentioned (as long as Yishtabach has not been said), or after the Amidah if Yishtabach has already been said.
The custom is to spread the palms (not raise the hands) when reciting this verse, and it is important to recite the concluding Hallel psalms gradually and with intention.

paragraphs: When one reaches the verses of ‘Vayevarech David,’ and says ‘Ve’atah Moshel BaKol’ [and You rule over all], he should give three perutot to charity, giving two together at once, and afterward the third; and there is a secret in this. Some are accustomed to give another three perutot in the same manner when saying ‘Ki Chol BaShamayim UvaAretz,’ in order to fulfill both traditions written by our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, and blessing will come upon him. A person should always strive to give his charity in this manner, so that it is two-thirds and one-third, and he should also be careful to give charity each time while standing, for there is a secret in this — to raise up the fallen sukkah of David. The most excellent form of charity is to give it into the hand of the gabbai [charity collector], and the gabbai gives it to the poor person, for this resembles the matter above, where Tiferet gives to Yesod and Yesod to Malchut — since the person corresponds to Tiferet, the gabbai corresponds to Yesod, and the poor person corresponds to Malchut. Therefore, when a poor person comes to his house to receive charity, he should give it into the hand of one of his household, who will hand it to the poor person, so that it be aligned according to the pattern above. He should also intend that there be a unification of the Name Havayah in it: the perutah corresponds to the yud, his five fingers and his arm correspond to the heh, vav, and the five fingers of the gabbai or the poor person correspond to the final heh of the Name. And when he says ‘Ve’atah Moshel BaKol,’ if there is no gabbai or poor person available before him, he should do as follows: he should ready in his lap one pouch, which is the charity pouch, and hold it with his left hand, and place the perutot with his right hand into this charity pouch, while holding it with his left hand — which stands in place of the gabbai or the poor person. And may the crown of my head, my father and teacher, of blessed and righteous memory, be remembered for good, who always kept a pouch in his lap from which he would set aside charity, several times a day, in large silver coins, to fulfill the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, in his commentary to the Mishnah in Avot, that everything depends on the frequency of the act; and afterward he would distribute from these coins that he set aside, several times each day, to the poor and for other mitzvot, to fulfill what our teacher Rabbi Moshe Alshich, of blessed memory, wrote at the beginning of Parashat Terumah — and he would read, over the entire portion [of charity given], for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, etc., to unify the Name and give satisfaction to his Creator — and all this with joy and with a willing heart. May his merit protect us, Amen.

clarification.explanation: When one reaches the verse ‘Ve’atah Moshel BaKol’ (in the chapter ‘Vayevarech David’), one should give three perutot to charity — two together, and then the third — and there is a secret in this. Some are accustomed to give another three perutot in the same manner when reaching the verse ‘Ki Chol BaShamayim UvaAretz,’ in order to fulfill both traditions written by Rabbi Chaim Vital. It is always proper to give charity in a manner of two-thirds and one-third (that is, two coins and then one), and to give the charity specifically while standing — there is a secret in this, of raising up the fallen sukkah of David. The most excellent form of charity is to give it into the hand of the gabbai, who gives it to the poor person — so that the act corresponds to the spiritual structure in which Tiferet gives to Yesod and Yesod gives to Malchut (the giver corresponds to Tiferet, the gabbai to Yesod, the poor person to Malchut). Therefore, if a poor person comes to his house, it is proper to hand the charity to one of the household members, who will pass it to the poor person, so as to preserve that same structure. There is likewise an intention regarding the unification of the Name Havayah at the moment of giving the coin: the perutah corresponds to the letter yud and the five fingers of the hand, the arm corresponds to heh and vav, and the palm of the gabbai or poor person corresponds to the final heh. If no gabbai or poor person is available at that moment, one should use a special charity pouch: holding it in the left hand (in place of the gabbai/poor person) and placing the perutot into it with the right hand. The Ben Ish Chai fondly recalls that his father was accustomed always to keep a charity pouch in his lap and to give charity from it several times a day in large silver coins, in order to fulfill the words of the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah in tractate Avot — that what matters most is the frequency of the acts of charity rather than the size of each sum — and afterward he would distribute from the money he had thus set aside each day to the poor and for other mitzvot. He was also accustomed, before this giving, to recite the declaration of unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, as Rabbi Moshe Alshich wrote at the beginning of Parashat Terumah, in order to unify the Name and give satisfaction to his Creator — and all this with joy and with a willing heart.
takeaways: At the verse ‘Ve’atah Moshel BaKol’ one gives three perutot to charity (two, then one), specifically while standing, and it is preferable to give through a gabbai rather than directly to the poor person.
There is a kabbalistic intention in the coin and the giving hand, corresponding to the sefirot of Tiferet-Yesod-Malchut and to the letters of the Name Havayah.

The Ben Ish Chai praises the practice of his father, who gave charity several times each day specifically (multiplying acts, as the Rambam teaches), with the intention of unifying the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah as taught by the Alshich, and all with joy.

paragraphs: The Song of the Sea should be said with joy and melody, as though standing within the sea at the time of the miracle, and this recitation is conducive to atonement for one’s sins. One should say the first ‘Mi Chamocha’ with a soft chaf (without dagesh), [and] the second ‘Umi Kamocha’ with a hard chaf (with dagesh); and likewise ‘Yidmu Ka’even’ with a hard chaf, so that it not appear as though one is saying ‘Yidmoch Even,’ Heaven forbid. One should also pause between ‘Bamayim’ and ‘Adirim,’ since the word ‘Adirim’ refers to the Egyptians. Also, ‘Am Zu Ga’alta’ — the gimel is hard [with dagesh], even though this is not, strictly speaking, grammatically correct, since the soft form is used in the sense of filth, as in ‘Lechem Mego’al’ (Malachi 1:7). Likewise one should be careful when saying ‘Ga’oh Ga’ah’ that the gimel be hard, as mentioned in Shalmei Tzibbur. And the verse ‘Hashem Yimloch’ should be said twice in the original text and once in Aramaic translation, as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: The Song of the Sea should be recited with joy and melody, as though standing within the sea at the moment of the miracle itself, and such recitation has the power to atone for sins. One must be precise in pronunciation: the first ‘Mi Chamocha’ — the chaf without dagesh, and the second — the chaf with dagesh; likewise ‘Yidmu Ka’even’ with a hard chaf, so that it should not sound, Heaven forbid, as though one is saying ‘Yidmoch’ (a term with a negative connotation). One should pause slightly between the words ‘Bamayim’ and ‘Adirim,’ since the word ‘Adirim’ refers to the Egyptians. Also ‘Am Zu Ga’alta’ — the gimel is hard, because with a soft pronunciation the word would carry a connotation of filth (as in ‘Lechem Mego’al’). Likewise in ‘Ga’oh Ga’ah’ one should pronounce the gimel with a dagesh. The verse ‘Hashem Yimloch’ should be said twice in the original Hebrew and once in Aramaic translation.
takeaways: The Song of the Sea is recited with joy, as though standing within the miracle itself, and this carries a special power for atonement of sins.
One must be precise in the pronunciation of certain words (Mi Chamocha, Yidmu Ka’even, Am Zu Ga’alta, Ga’oh Ga’ah) so as not to inadvertently change their meaning.

paragraphs: The praise of the blessing of Yishtabach is exceedingly great and awesome; some say that Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, instituted it, and some say that its beginning was instituted by King Solomon, peace be upon him, while the blessing itself was instituted by Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him. These thirteen praises of ‘Shir U’Shevachah’ correspond to the Thirteen Attributes of ‘Kel Rachum,’ and one must recite them with melody, as one who arranges the praise of a king; therefore one should not say them in a single breath, as is the custom of some people. And I found it written that one should count them on his fingers, and this is a correct and proper practice, and so I am accustomed to do. As for the law of answering Kaddish, Kedushah, and the like in the middle of the blessing of Yishtabach — its law is as I wrote above regarding the blessing of Baruch She’amar. However, one must be careful not to bring himself to the point of interruption for Kaddish, Kedushah, and the like, within the thirteen praises of ‘Shir U’Shevachah’; rather, if he sees that the congregation is about to say so, he should wait until he can answer with them, and only afterward begin the thirteen praises. And if it happens to him suddenly, in the midst of the thirteen praises, that he is forced to interrupt, then after he answers the Kaddish and the like, he should go back and begin them from the start — that is, he should return to say ‘Ki Lecha Na’eh Hashem Eloheinu VeElohei Avoteinu Shir U’Shevachah,’ etc. — so that he may say the thirteen praises without any interruption in between.

clarification.explanation: The blessing of Yishtabach is an exceedingly great and exalted praise. Some say Avraham Avinu instituted it, while others say King Solomon instituted its beginning, and Avraham Avinu instituted the blessing itself. The thirteen expressions of praise (‘Shir VeShivcha, Hallel VeZimrah,’ etc.) correspond to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy (‘Kel Rachum’). One should recite them with melody, as one who arranges the praise before a king, and not in a single breath as some people do — rather, counting them on the fingers, a correct and good practice. Regarding the law of answering Kaddish and Kedushah in the middle of the blessing of Yishtabach — it is identical to what was said regarding Baruch She’amar. However, one must take special care not to bring himself into a situation of interruption within the thirteen expressions of praise: if he sees the congregation about to answer, he should wait until he answers with them and only then begin the thirteen praises; and if the interruption comes upon him suddenly in the midst of them, after he answers he must go back and begin them again from ‘Ki Lecha Na’eh,’ in order to say them in one uninterrupted sequence.
takeaways: The thirteen expressions of praise in Yishtabach correspond to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, and should be recited with melody, not in haste.
One must be careful not to interrupt in the middle of the thirteen praises; if forced to, one must go back and begin them again after answering.

paragraphs: Here in our city, may it be protected, the custom is for all the Kaddishes in the prayer service, including the Kaddish of Barechu after Yishtabach, to be said by the men who recite Kaddish for their deceased. And there is much distress caused by the failings that arise from this, for among them are many ignorant and unlearned people who do not know how to fulfill the congregation’s obligation. Moreover, they recite the Kaddish very quickly, actually skipping words. What can I say and what can I add about the failings that arise from this matter, which cannot be put into writing. And praised be God, several years ago I instituted a new custom here in our city: that on Shabbat and Yom Tov the cantor himself recites the Kaddish of Barechu, for previously the custom was for the cantor to recite this Kaddish only on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. And praised be God, this custom has become established on Shabbatot and Yamim Tovim, and although this matter was difficult for the congregation to accept in their hearts, since they thought that by reciting this Kaddish they were bringing the dead to life, nevertheless they remained silent and accepted this, with the help of Hashem, and it was a small measure of relief. But regarding the Kaddish of Barechu on weekdays, I did not change anything, and it remains until now that those who recite Kaddish for their deceased during their year [of mourning] or on the anniversary [Yahrzeit] recite this Kaddish.

Now it sometimes happens that those who are reciting this Kaddish are still in the middle of the zemirot, while the prayer leader has already concluded the blessing of Yishtabach, he and the congregation, and they are standing ready to say the Kaddish of Barechu. I discussed this matter at length in my holy work Rav Pe’alim, and there I concluded, with the help of Heaven, that since this Kaddish was instituted for the needs of the congregation’s prayer — that they require the Kaddish after they finish the prayer of Yetzirah, which is the zemirot — and this person reciting Kaddish is already standing within the zemirot, reciting it on behalf of the congregation in place of the prayer leader, we have no basis to protest against those who recite this Kaddish while still within the zemirot that have not yet been completed. And regarding the concern of improper interruption, I also concluded there that there is no concern. Nevertheless, although I wrote that one should not protest, certainly the meticulous should not act in this way, and they should not recite this Kaddish unless they have finished Yishtabach.

clarification.explanation: In Baghdad it was customary that all the Kaddishes of the prayer service, including the Kaddish of Barechu after Yishtabach, were recited by those saying Kaddish in memory of their deceased relatives. The Ben Ish Chai describes great distress that many of those reciting it are ignorant and unlearned and do not know how to properly discharge the congregation’s obligation, and that they recite it hastily, skipping words. He recounts that several years earlier he instituted a new custom: on Shabbat and Yom Tov the cantor himself would recite the Kaddish of Barechu (whereas previously the custom was to say it this way only on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur), and although this was difficult for the congregation, who thought that their own recitation of this Kaddish benefited the souls of the departed, they ultimately accepted it. However, he did not change the weekday Kaddish of Barechu, and it remained the practice that those in mourning or observing a Yahrzeit recite it. It sometimes happens that the person reciting this Kaddish is still in the midst of the zemirot when the cantor and congregation have already finished Yishtabach and are ready to say the Kaddish of Barechu. The Ben Ish Chai discusses this at length in his work Rav Pe’alim and concludes that one should not protest against such a person continuing to recite Kaddish while still in the zemirot, since the Kaddish was instituted for the congregation’s needs after the zemirot, and he is effectively saying it on their behalf in place of the cantor — and there is likewise no concern of improper interruption. Nevertheless, the meticulous should not do this, and should wait until they have finished Yishtabach.
takeaways: The Ben Ish Chai’s innovation: on Shabbat and Yom Tov the cantor himself recites the Kaddish of Barechu, not only on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur as in the old custom.

One who is reciting Kaddish in memory of a deceased relative and is still in the midst of the zemirot when the congregation reaches the Kaddish of Barechu should not be protested against, but the meticulous will wait until they have finished Yishtabach.

paragraphs: The one who recites the Kaddish of Barechu should also say ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach Le’olam Va’ed’ himself, and should not turn his face away until he has finished saying ‘Baruch Hashem,’ etc. And if a person did not hear the ‘Barechu’ said by the one reciting the Kaddish, but heard only the congregation answering ‘Baruch Hashem,’ etc. — some say that he should answer Amen after them; and some say that he too should say ‘Baruch Hashem,’ etc., together with them. And in my holy work Makabtziel, I concluded, with the help of Heaven, that he should answer ‘Baruch Hashem,’ etc., together with them.

clarification.explanation: The one reciting the Kaddish of Barechu must himself also say ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach Le’olam Va’ed,’ and should not turn away his face until he finishes saying this. One who did not hear the Barechu recited by the one saying Kaddish himself, but heard only the congregation answering ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach’ — some say he should answer only ‘Amen,’ and some say he should say ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach’ together with the congregation. The Ben Ish Chai ruled in his work Makabtziel that one should say ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach’ together with the congregation.
takeaways: One who did not hear the Barechu directly from the one reciting Kaddish, but only the congregation’s response, should say ‘Baruch Hashem HaMevorach Le’olam Va’ed’ together with the congregation, not merely Amen.

paragraphs: The Acharonim wrote: when praying alone, one should recite the following baraita after Yishtabach: Rabbi Akiva said: There stands a creature (chayah) in the firmament, and its name is Yisrael, and ‘Yisrael’ is engraved upon its forehead; it stands in the midst of the firmament and proclaims: ‘Bless Hashem, the blessed One’; and all the heavenly hosts answer and say: ‘Blessed is Hashem, the blessed One, forever and ever.’

And in my holy work Makabtziel I wrote that one should not interrupt with this passage between Yishtabach and Yotzer, even under great duress, unlike what is written in Chesed LeAvraham; rather, one should say this passage before ‘Aleinu LeShabeach’ [at the end of the service], and likewise at the beginning of the Ma’ariv prayer before the blessing.

clarification.explanation: The Acharonim wrote that one praying alone should recite, after Yishtabach, the words of Rabbi Akiva: concerning a creature (chayah) in the firmament called ‘Yisrael,’ with ‘Yisrael’ engraved on its forehead, standing in the midst of the firmament and proclaiming ‘Bless Hashem, the blessed One,’ and all the heavenly hosts answering ‘Blessed is Hashem, the blessed One, forever and ever.’ The Ben Ish Chai wrote in his work Makabtziel that one should not interrupt to recite this baraita between Yishtabach and Yotzer, even under great duress — unlike the position of Chesed LeAvraham — but should instead say it before ‘Aleinu LeShabeach’ [at the end of Shacharit], and likewise at the beginning of the Ma’ariv prayer, before its blessing.
takeaways: The words of Rabbi Akiva about the ‘creature named Yisrael’ are recited by an individual not within the prayer service itself (between Yishtabach and Yotzer), but before Aleinu LeShabeach at the end of Shacharit, and before the blessing at the beginning of Ma’ariv.
